In the vast expanse of the universe, where stars spiral like the petals of a nebulae, and galaxies dance in the quiet solitude of endless voids, there lies the story of a small, seemingly inconspicuous planet. This planet, Earth, is but one among trillions, yet its uniqueness in terms of habitability and the life that thrives upon it makes it the centerpiece of a narrative woven across centuries and epochs. 

Our story begins in the mists of prehistory, where the first stirrings of life emerged on this planet. It was not a momentous event, seeping into cracks in the oily, black skin of our soot-swirled world, but a gradual, almost imperceptible phase transition, where the capacity for replication, differentiation, and ultimately, consciousness, became the markers of a new form of being. This was the dawn of life, a primer upon which humanity would later add its particular hue and passion.

The age of dinosaurs, with its titanic struggles and catastrophic endings, was a backdrop to the slow, cautious ascent of the apes. In the coliseums of prehistoric forests, the first primate with bipedal locomotion, with a mind capable of abstract thought and the rudiments of speech, was a leap that would determine the path not just of itself, but of all that followed. This was the age of the ancestors, the flickering forth and back of human evolution, a process that unfolded in fits and starts, punctuated by epochs of slumber and wakefulness.

The first humans walked the Acacus, lungs gasping for air in the atmosphere of a world very much like their own, but slightly different, teeming with creatures that roamed in the twilight of the gloom, beasts that walked on two legs, like them, but alien in every sense. The human story, which began with the first breaths and the first tentative steps, was a sequential narrative of exploration and discovery, of striving and suffering, of conquering and losing, of loss and finding.

The ilithid smiled cruelly as they cast aside the hollow husks of the great kings and queens of the surface dwellers. Their breeding ground, their perfect laboratory for the next phase of their master's science, lay in the dark and the depths. They faced down the locathah with an ease that bespoke their intelligence, their researchers, soldiers, and diplomats, united in purpose by the end they sought. The crimson sun cast long shadows across the surface of their new domain, a shadow that fell upon the remnants of humanity and the very fabric of the world itself.

Humanity, like the rest of life on Earth, wrested from the prehistoric in favor of the new. Butterflies grew paler, as did the forest, surrendered to the encroachments of the human from the trees. Creatures that fed upon the fronds, the detritus, relinquished their place in the grim circle of life to creatures that walked on legs, that towered, that fed more amply, more deeply, than any.

Industries were born, and the achievement of beings that descended from fire and bones, the only progress unknown to the dragonborn, was a herald of doom for the nature they revered that once stood prairie and veld. Cuts laid open the belly of the earth; fumes rose to the heavens and worked the air, the air, a raw, unheard element that now rionded the skies with sulfurous storms. The children of Gaia, seekers of knowledge and discovery, stumbled upon the beast from the hole, and with it, the name of death the bard sang.

The dawn of the industrial age, when humans began terra-forming, not just of their own lands, but also their planet, changed the essence of their existence. The old gods of the wild, cured of their power and stripped of their dominion, now wandered among the legions of lost souls. Chaos, born of innovation and progress, faced down inversion with indifference, dragging humans through a morass of physical and psychological ailments, of supernatural and natural horrors, of a new breed of spirit rulers who sought not dominion but altruism, a 'love-filled realm,' as they called it. But this 'happy-everything' was a sweet descent into madness, a whirl wind of sonder and despair, a vortex of nightmares.

The world awoke to revelations of despair and fear. Shattered worlds, strange magics, and unearthings of a previously glorified world led to a cacophony of conflict. Cities crumbled, turning back into forests, powering, and despair. Cities crumbled, turning back into forests, contaminating their air, and despair. The survivors fought for their lives, guided by a Gith trust in their leadership, but hope was waning, replaced by a blind, raging fury directed at two extraterrestrial bêtes noires—whatever they were, they were Monster. For the first time since the discovery of this world, Monsters made the headlines as the only hope humanity had to escape and preserve their future.

An arc of transformation spanned from the Dark Suns towards the Pharaoh of the Nile. Time unfurled, bending on its winds, the very fabric of reality seeping into and through the cracks. The Pharaoh tasked the kingdom's scholars to uncover the Rock of Shadows and understand its mysterious powers, forever changing the fate of the land and the world. Yet, simultaneous with this, a price was being exacted for humanity's hubris. A thousand patches appeared under the sun, a thousand microcosms of transformed natural landscapes. In these zones, the deceased rose, the heat kith changed their forms, Nethys himself roamed the lands, and the dread and inescapable aesthetic of the Undermountain spread to the world.

From the depths of Shadowfell, a creature stumbled, lost, disoriented, and conflicting. Known as the Venerer, a round beast covered in fat and sinew, it sought only sustenance, food, and a world to call its own. It chased the moon towards the east, laughing as it did so, a bone-chilling cackle that resonated through the realms. Instead of finding friends, the Venerer found troubles. More troubles scurried after the moon, chased shadows, and it was then that it was discovered. It was known, first by Terror, and then by Destroyer. Was it a benevolent being, one that would open the floodgates to Tartarus and insure its own death, or was it a harbinger of the gods' end, a destroyer of worlds and a bringer of chaos?

The Word of Soaring, Viashino descent Taeriv, flees the Kingdom, bound for the lands of Solis. The only source of knowledge that would save humanity had vanished, bound for the skies, a plane of perpetual light and beauty. In Solis, he found his wife, Anaral. To him, she was a god, a goddess of beauty beyond measure, and a being of awe-inspiring power and influence. Together, they traveled the planes, their heroes on their shoulders, together bringing oblivion to their foes. Yet, as the term 'opposites attract' attests, the union faced skepticism, misunderstanding, and speculation, foreshadowing the profound tragedy that would befall the heroes of Solis.

The thrill of flight, the ethereal bonds of love, the dawn of a new era, Seventeen books of Barzell, a howl from the starless heavens demanded, "If you are a traveler amongst the planes in search of your destiny, tey will draw you into the fray of destiny." Behind and beyond the edge of existence, Death walks with step of steel, and in his hands, holds a key to birth, a hatchling's egg, yet another, a gift of an eden shattered. This was the end, but not to the first Remnant, the cradle that suspended a shattered cosmos.
